name: Maricopa
confidence_why: Gordon 1986, the only full grammar, puts stress by rule on the final vowel of the root, and Langdon 1977 and Geary 2022 say the same for Yuman as a whole, so final stress is secure for the ordinary unsuffixed word, but all three note that stress stays on the root when an unstressed syllabic suffix follows, which a strictly word-final coding does not show.
catalog_quote: Stress is assigned by rule on the final vowel of the root. This is the same general rule found in other Yuman languages. (Gordon 1986:9)

new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. [...] Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes. [...] Nevertheless, suffixes producing unstressed syllables are common, though they are mostly syntactic in function. (p. 239) — Note that regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root. The only thing that can happen to a stressed syllable is that the stress reduces in compound formation to secondary stress on the first member of the compound, thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable. (p. 240)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records fixed final stress. Langdon agrees that Yuman words tend to be stressed on the last syllable, but attributes this to root stress plus heavy prefixation, and notes that unstressed syntactic suffixes commonly follow the stressed root, so 'fixed final' is the surface tendency of uninflected words rather than a phonological rule. The statement is family-wide; Maricopa itself is only named in the classification and gets no data or example.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement covering all ten Yuman languages, Maricopa included (River group with Mojave and Yuma): word stress is morphological, fixed on the (typically monosyllabic) root; because Yuman words are built mostly by prefixation, uninflected words usually end up with final stress, but syntactic suffixes can add unstressed post-stress syllables, so final position is a tendency, not the rule. Conclusion p. 252: 'Stress is basically morphological, it is a property of the root'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In compounds the first member's root stress reduces to secondary stress (and may reduce further to unstressed), keeping primary stress on the last member (p. 240). Footnote 4 (p. 257): some investigators (Redden 1966, Halpern 1946-47) describe suffixes carrying primary stress, so some Yuman 'words' have two primary stresses; Langdon treats these as two words.
new_statements.exceptions: Mojave alone shows perceived stress retraction onto a pre-root syllable conditioned by vowel length (pp. 248-252), explicitly described as 'unique among Yuman languages'; nothing of the kind is reported for Maricopa. Kiliwa, Paipai and Yavapai have (marginal) pitch contrasts; Maricopa is not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Langdon 1977 treats Maricopa only as a member of the River group (with Mojave and Yuma) of Yuman; the paper's language-specific data come from Diegueno, Cocopa, Kiliwa, Walapai, Paipai, Yavapai and Mojave, not from Maricopa. Spier 1946 (Havasupai and Maricopa vocabularies and texts) was not opened.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. The catalog's StressTyp2 record codes Maricopa as fixed final stress; the one source opened (Langdon 1977) says, for the whole Yuman family, that stress is morphological and sits on the root, which yields final stress in uninflected words because Yuman morphology is prefixing, while unstressed syntactic suffixes may follow the root. The two accounts describe the same surface pattern at different levels (phonological final vs. morphological root); Langdon's is the more explanatory one but is family-level and contains no Maricopa data. Spier 1946 could not be opened, so nothing from it bears on the question.

audit.recode_to: morphological (root-final stress: primary stress on the last vowel of the root regardless of affixes; surface-final only when no syllabic suffix follows) — or at minimum fixed-dominant final with a root-stress caution, matching how the catalog treats Cocopa (coco1261) and Jamul Tiipay (kumi1248) on equivalent statements
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim at Gordon 1986:9 in the page scan we hold. (2) Source: 1986 reference grammar, the best and only full description; held for the relevant pages. (3) But the classification does not follow from the quote. sources.quote: Das Vorwalten consonantischer Ausgänge der Wörter ist charakteristisch, tritt aber auch beim Kutchan zu Tage. Die Oxytonirung tritt bei Ten Kate weit mehr hervor, als in den Vocabularien von Whipple und Bartlett.
sources.note: The only accent statement in the work: final-syllable (oxytone) accent is far more prominent in Ten Kate's 1888 Maricopa vocabulary than in Whipple's and Bartlett's. It is a compiler's observation on how one transcriber marked accent, not a rule of the language; weak evidence for predominantly final accent in Maricopa words as heard in 1888. Catalog entry for mari1440 (Gordon 1986, classification morphological, rule empty) is not contradicted.

sources.note: The paper is a syntactic/semantic study of the Maricopa 'say' auxiliary ?i (intentionality 'try to/want to' after main verbs; immediacy in progressive auxiliary constructions; question readings with non-nY demonstratives). It contains no statement of the word-stress or accent system, no stress marks in the transcriptions, and nothing on tone. The only prosody-adjacent remarks are an impressionistic note that a sentence-internal /i/ 'sounds overloud', a mention of 'rising interrogative intonation' in WH questions, and 'forceful delivery' annotations on examples (31'-31'').
